reason: Attacked at the punctuation, which is where this line usually fails, and it held. I pulled the raw page source of the Wikisource scan the verifier cites (Page:Aurora Leigh a Poem.djvu/313, https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Page:Aurora_Leigh_a_Poem.djvu/313&action=raw) rather than a rendered transcription, so nothing was normalised in between. The six lines read there exactly as shipped: Earth’s crammed with heaven, / And every common bush afire with God: / But only he who sees, takes off his shoes, / The rest sit round it, and pluck blackberries, / And daub their natural faces unaware / More and more, from the first similitude. The colon after God and the comma after shoes are both in the scan, and the apostrophe in Earth’s is already curly in the source, so the verifier’s correction of the proposal’s semicolon is right and not the other way round. The edition is right too: the Index page for that scan gives Publisher=Chapman and Hall, Address=London, Year=1857, which is the first edition named. The Book is right: Aurora Leigh/Seventh Book transcludes pages 284 to 330, and 313 sits inside it. The speaker is right: the same leaf carries I, Aurora, still three lines below the quotation, so this is Aurora’s own narration and the parenthetical (Aurora) is correct rather than decorative. Scope, cap and novelty all clear: shipped.js returns no exact hit, no near hit, Browning at one line for the year (month 3), not banned. Tag Poetry is the form of the work. Source line is 86 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight quote; the quotation ends in a full stop. Two caveats that do not amount to a refutation but should travel with the line. First, the Wikisource page carries pagequality level 1, meaning not proofread, so it is bot OCR of the page image; every reading it gives matches the passage as standardly printed, and the disagreements between editions in this passage are exactly the two marks I checked, so I am confident, but nobody has laid eyes on the physical leaf. Second, the quotation opens in the middle of a verse line: the edition’s line reads Doth utter itself distinct. Earth’s crammed with heaven, so the card’s first slash segment is a half line, and Earth is capitalised as a noun, not as a line head. The verifier’s note already says this plainly, which is what the standard asks for. The burning bush is literary allusion inside a verse novel, not scripture, so the Library rule is not engaged.
